candidate.answerReason: There are 70 crossing pairs of diagonals. Exactly eight noncentral points have three diagonals through them, and the center has four. Correcting these multiplicities gives 70-8(3-1)-(6-1)=49, agreeing with A.

methods.label: Count crossing pairs and correct repeated points
methods.explanation:
Choosing four vertices gives a convex quadrilateral whose two diagonals cross inside the octagon. Conversely, every crossing pair of diagonals determines exactly four vertices. Thus the number of crossing pairs is
\[
\binom{8}{4}=70.
\]
This counts pairs of diagonals rather than distinct points. If several diagonals meet at one point, we must replace their several pair counts by a single point count.

Label the vertices \(V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_7\) in cyclic order, and let \(O\) be the center. Diagonals sharing a vertex cannot also meet in the interior, so diagonals through a common interior point have distinct endpoints. Consequently, at most four diagonals can meet there.

If four diagonals meet, each diagonal must have one endpoint of each of the other three diagonals on each side of it. Its endpoints therefore have three vertices between them in each direction around the octagon, so they are opposite vertices. Thus four diagonals meet only at \(O\), where the four diameters intersect.

To find every possible triple intersection, consider its six endpoints, written in cyclic order as \(A_1,\ldots,A_6\). Each diagonal must separate the endpoints of the other two, so the only possible three diagonals are
\[
A_1A_4,\qquad A_2A_5,\qquad A_3A_6.
\]
We can therefore classify triples by the two octagon vertices omitted from their endpoints. Rotation and reflection reduce the possibilities to omitted vertices \(V_0,V_d\), where \(d=1,2,3,4\).

We will use the following symmetry fact: two crossing diagonals that are reflections of one another meet on the reflecting axis. Their unique intersection must be fixed by that reflection.

For \(d=1\), the possible triple is \(V_2V_5,V_3V_6,V_4V_7\). The first two are reflections across diameter \(V_0V_4\), so their crossing lies on that diameter. But \(V_4V_7\) meets the diameter only at the boundary vertex \(V_4\). There is no triple intersection.

For \(d=2\), the possible triple is \(V_1V_5,V_3V_6,V_4V_7\). The last two cross and are reflections across diameter \(V_1V_5\), so their crossing lies on that diameter. These three diagonals do meet. Their point is not \(O\), because the last two diagonals are not diameters.

For \(d=3\), the possible triple is \(V_1V_5,V_2V_6,V_4V_7\). The first two are diameters and meet at \(O\), while the third does not pass through \(O\). There is no triple intersection.

For \(d=4\), the possible triple is \(V_1V_5,V_2V_6,V_3V_7\). These are three diameters, giving the already identified center.

There are eight omitted pairs of the form \(\{V_i,V_{i+2}\}\), with indices read cyclically, so there are eight noncentral triple intersections. They are distinct: if two different triples met at the same noncentral point, at least four diagonals would meet there, which we have ruled out. The cases above exhaust all triples, so every remaining intersection has exactly two diagonals through it.

Each triple intersection contributed \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) to our pair count instead of \(1\), and the center contributed \(\binom{4}{2}=6\) instead of \(1\). Hence the number of distinct interior intersection points is
\[
70-8(3-1)-(6-1)=\boxed{49}.
\]
The answer is \(\text{A}\).
